title: Row Space, Column Space, Null Space (4.7)
description: Definitions and computation of the row space, column space, and null space of a matrix, the Rank-Nullity Theorem, and what each space means. 8 questions pulled per attempt from a pool of 30.

questions.prompt: For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the column space $\text{col}(A)$ is a subspace of _____.
questions.explanation: Each column of $A$ has $m$ entries, so every linear combination of the columns — every vector in $\text{col}(A)$ — lives in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

questions.prompt: For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the row space $\text{row}(A)$ is a subspace of _____.
questions.explanation: Each row of $A$ has $n$ entries, so $\text{row}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ — the same space the solution vector $x$ lives in.

questions.prompt: For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the null space $\text{null}(A)$ is a subspace of _____.
questions.explanation: $\text{null}(A)$ is the solution set of $Ax=0$, and $x$ is an $n \times 1$ vector, so $\text{null}(A) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ — the same space as $\text{row}(A)$, but note it's a different subspace of that space.

questions.prompt: $\text{col}(A)$ is best described as...
choices: the set of all vectors b for which Ax = b is consistent
the span of the rows of A
the set of pivot columns in the RREF of A
always equal to all of R^m
explanations: That description is row(A), not col(A).
The RREF's own columns are generally not even in col(A) — pivot columns must come from the original matrix A.
col(A) only fills up all of R^m when A has rank m; otherwise it's a smaller subspace.

questions.prompt: $\text{null}(A)$ is best described as...
choices: the set of all x such that Ax = 0
the set of all b such that Ax = b is consistent
the pivot columns of A
the same subspace as row(A) in general
explanations: That's col(A), not null(A).
Pivot columns of A form a basis for col(A), not null(A).
row(A) and null(A) are both subspaces of R^n, but they are generally different subspaces (they only share the zero vector).

questions.prompt: To find a basis for null(A), you...
choices: row reduce A, then solve Ax = 0, writing the general solution in terms of the free variables
take the nonzero rows of the RREF of A
take the pivot columns of A
take the pivot columns of the RREF of A
explanations: That gives a basis for row(A), not null(A).
That gives a basis for col(A), not null(A).
The RREF's columns aren't the right objects here — null(A) comes from solving Ax=0, not from picking columns.

questions.prompt: To find a basis for col(A), you...
choices: row reduce A to find which columns are pivot columns, then take those SAME columns from the ORIGINAL matrix A
take the pivot columns directly from the RREF of A
take the nonzero rows of the RREF of A
solve Ax = 0 and use the free variables
explanations: This is the classic trap: row reduction changes which vectors the columns actually are. The RREF tells you WHICH columns to grab (by position), but you grab them from A itself.
That gives a basis for row(A), not col(A).
That's how you find null(A), not col(A).

questions.prompt: To find a basis for row(A), you...
choices: row reduce A to RREF; the nonzero rows of the RREF form a basis
take the pivot columns of A
solve Ax = 0 and use the free variables
take the nonzero columns of A
explanations: That gives a basis for col(A), not row(A).
That gives a basis for null(A), not row(A).
Columns of A (zero or not) relate to col(A), not row(A).

questions.prompt: True or False: row(A) = row(RREF(A)) — row reduction never changes the row space.
choices: True
False
explanations: Each row of the RREF is a linear combination of A's original rows, and since row operations are reversible, each original row is also a combination of the RREF's rows. So the two row spaces are exactly the same set.

questions.prompt: True or False: col(A) = col(RREF(A)) — row reduction never changes the column space.
choices: True
False
explanations: This is false, and it's exactly why the pivot-column rule matters: row operations mix rows together, which generally changes what the columns actually are as vectors. Only the DIMENSION of col(A) (the rank) is preserved — not the space itself. That's why a basis for col(A) has to be pulled from A's own columns, never from the RREF's columns.

questions.prompt: True or False: null(A) = null(RREF(A)).
choices: True
False
explanations: This is the entire point of row reduction: elementary row operations never change the solution set of Ax = 0. So A and its RREF always have exactly the same null space.

questions.prompt: True or False: dim(row(A)) always equals dim(col(A)), even though row(A) and col(A) are generally subspaces of different spaces (R^n vs R^m).
choices: True
False
explanations: True — this shared dimension (the number of pivots) is called the rank of A.

questions.prompt: The Rank-Nullity Theorem: for an m x n matrix A, rank(A) + nullity(A) = _____.
questions.explanation: Every one of the n columns is either a pivot column (contributing to rank) or a free-variable column (contributing to nullity) — together they account for all n columns.

questions.prompt: A is a 5x8 matrix with rank 3. Find nullity(A).
A is a 4x6 matrix with nullity 2. Find rank(A).
A is a 7x3 matrix with rank 3 (full column rank). Find nullity(A).
questions.explanation: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n = 3, so nullity(A) = 3 - 3 = 0 — the only solution to Ax=0 is x=0.

questions.prompt: If null(A) = {0} (only the zero vector), what does that tell you about Ax = b?
choices: Whenever Ax = b is consistent, the solution is unique
Ax = b is never consistent, for any b
Ax = b always has infinitely many solutions
A must be a square matrix
explanations: null(A) = {0} says nothing about whether a given b is reachable — it only controls uniqueness once a solution exists.
Infinitely many solutions is exactly what CAN'T happen when null(A) = {0}: two different solutions to Ax=b would differ by a nonzero vector in null(A).
A can be any shape; null(A) = {0} just means the columns of A are linearly independent, which is possible for tall or square matrices.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$ (today's in-class example), find rank(A).
questions.explanation: The RREF has 2 pivots (columns 1 and 3), so rank(A) = 2.

questions.prompt: For the same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$, find nullity(A).
questions.explanation: n = 4 columns, rank = 2, so nullity = 4 - 2 = 2 — matches the two free variables (columns 2 and 4) and the two basis vectors we found for null(A) in class.

questions.prompt: For the same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$, find dim(col(A)).
questions.explanation: dim(col(A)) is always equal to rank(A) = 2 — col(A) is spanned by the 2 pivot columns of A, columns 1 and 3.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, find rank(A).
questions.explanation: Row-reducing gives 2 nonzero rows (row 3 becomes all zeros — it's a combination of the first two), so rank(A) = 2.

questions.prompt: For the same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, find nullity(A).
questions.explanation: n = 3 columns, rank = 2, so nullity = 3 - 2 = 1 — a single free variable, giving a 1-dimensional null space.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, find dim(row(A)).
questions.explanation: Row 2 is just 2 times Row 1, so it disappears under row reduction — only 1 nonzero row survives, so dim(row(A)) = rank(A) = 1.

questions.prompt: For the same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, find dim(null(A)).
questions.explanation: n = 3 columns, rank = 1, so nullity = 3 - 1 = 2 — two free variables.

questions.prompt: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ and $b = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}$. Is $b$ in $\text{col}(A)$?
choices: Yes, b is in col(A)
No, b is not in col(A)
explanations: b is in col(A) exactly when Ax = b is consistent. Here it is (x = (1, 1) works: 1(1,2,3) + 1(2,4,5) = (3,6,8)), so b ∈ col(A).

questions.prompt: Same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$, now with $b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Is $b$ in $\text{col}(A)$?
choices: Yes, b is in col(A)
No, b is not in col(A)
explanations: Row reducing [A | b] shows an inconsistent row (rank(A) = 2 but rank([A|b]) = 3), so Ax = b has no solution — b is NOT in col(A).

questions.prompt: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$. Is $v$ in $\text{null}(A)$?
choices: Yes, v is in null(A)
No, v is not in null(A)

questions.prompt: Same $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, now with $v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Is $v$ in $\text{null}(A)$?
choices: Yes, v is in null(A)
No, v is not in null(A)
explanations: Av = (1+3-2, 2+1+1) = (2, 4) ≠ (0,0), so v is NOT in null(A). Checking membership in null(A) is easy — just multiply and see if you get 0.

questions.prompt: True or False: the zero vector is always in null(A), no matter what A is.
choices: True
False
explanations: A(0) = 0 for every matrix A, so the zero vector is always a solution to Ax=0 — null(A) is never empty.

questions.prompt: True or False: the zero vector is always in col(A).
choices: True
False
explanations: col(A) is a span of vectors, and every span (every subspace) contains the zero vector — take all coefficients to be 0.
